title: After the morning
hookLine: then, as the day rises, the Sikh sings the Guru's word and remembers, sitting and standing (Gauri Var M4, ang 305)

cards: The prayers are finished. The tea is gone. Someone can't find a shoe, the inbox has filled up overnight, and the bus is already at the corner.
A quiet morning can last about as long as it takes to open the front door. After that, the day takes over, and by lunch the early hours can feel like they happened to somebody else.
Guru Ram Das's salok doesn't end at sunrise. Its second half begins with a small, important word: then.

teach.h: THE MORNING IS WHERE IT STARTS.
teach.b: Here's the second half, paraphrased. Then, as the day rises, he sings the Guru's word.
Sitting and standing, he dwells on the Name. The one who remembers the Lord with every breath and every bite, that Gursikh is pleasing to the Guru's mind. Start with then.
The morning is a beginning, not the whole of it: the place where remembering gets lit, like a fire, not where it gets finished and put away. Next, sitting and standing.
That's the posture of a whole day: at a desk, behind a counter, in a car, on your feet in a kitchen.
Some readers hear in it the Sikh teaching of honest work, kirat karni: the Sikh isn't asked to leave the job to remember, but to remember inside it.
Then the measure: saas giraas, breath and mouthful, the smallest units a day has. Breaths and bites just keep happening, all day long. So remembering here isn't a block of time you schedule.
It's a thread through the things you do anyway. And notice who the salok says is pleased. Not the boss, not the neighbors, not someone keeping score of who prayed longest.
That quietly changes what a good working day is: not only what got done, but whether the Name came along while it got done.

how: Sikh teaching joins remembering the Name with honest work, kirat karni; Sikhs who keep it repeat Waheguru or hum a line of Gurbani through the working day rather than setting the day apart from prayer.

o: a nap Sikhs take once the morning prayers end
keeping the Name close through the working day

games.q: the second half of the salok: tap the pairs.
p: the morning is only the start

games.q: the morning prayers are done and the workday is starting. what does the salok picture next?
o: leave work behind to keep praying.
sing the Guru's word, and remember sitting and standing.
save remembering for the next morning.
games.why: then, as the day rises, he sings the Guru's word, and sitting and standing, dwells on the Name.

practice: Run through your working day in your mind, where you sit, where you stand, what you eat, and choose one thing that happens again and again, sitting down, a sip of water, a door, as your cue.
Each time it comes, one slower breath can remember, silently, with Waheguru if you pray.

wordCard.voice: After the morning. The second half of the salok: then sing the Guru's word, and sitting and standing, with breath and mouthful, keep the Name close. Today's word.

orig.note: with breath and mouthful: the salok's measure for remembering through the day.

carryVoice: Your line: work, remembering. The Name can come along while the hands keep working. Rest well.

sources.ref: Guru Granth Sahib, Gauri ki Var, salok Mahala 4, Ang 305 (then as the day rises he sings Gurbani; sitting and standing he dwells on the Name; with every breath and mouthful he remembers, and pleases the Guru's mind)
